questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Reading a Constitution Philosophically' refers to.
questions.a: Beyond its legal clauses, every constitution carries a philosophy -- core convictions about freedom, equality and political community. Reading philosophically means asking what vision the text serves, how its parts cohere, and whether its promises have been kept in practice, treating the Constitution as a political tradition to be argued with, not just applied.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Reading a Constitution Philosophically'.
questions.a: Every clause encodes an idea -- philosophy reads the Constitution for its convictions, not just its rules.

concepts.title: The Constituent Assembly Debates as Source of Philosophy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Constituent Assembly Debates as Source of Philosophy' refers to.
questions.a: The Constituent Assembly's recorded debates are the richest window into the Constitution's intent: members disagreed over village republics versus central strength, language, minority safeguards and property. These arguments show the text as a set of negotiated answers, and later generations can reopen the arguments using the same reasons.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Constituent Assembly Debates as Source of Philosophy'.
questions.a: The debates hand every generation the reasons behind each clause -- the raw material for constitutional argument.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Constituent Assembly Debates as Source of Philosophy' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Core Values: Freedom, Equality, Justice and Fraternity in the Design

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Core Values: Freedom, Equality, Justice and Fraternity in the Design' refers to.
questions.a: The Constitution's philosophy rests on interlocking values. Freedom appears as individual liberties protected against the state; equality as both formal equality before law and enabling provisions for the disadvantaged; justice as social and economic transformation through directive principles; fraternity as the dignity and unity that make the others livable in a diverse society.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Core Values: Freedom, Equality, Justice and Fraternity in the Design'.
questions.a: Liberty, equality, justice and fraternity are not slogans -- each is wired into structures, rights and directives.

concepts.title: Institutional Vision: Parliamentary, Federal and Secular Design

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Institutional Vision: Parliamentary, Federal and Secular Design' refers to.
questions.a: The philosophy shows in institutional choices: a parliamentary executive fuses responsibility and accountability; federalism with a strong centre holds a vast diversity together while honouring regional identity; a secular state with equal respect for religions answers a multi-faith society; an independent judiciary anchors rights above majorities.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Institutional Vision: Parliamentary, Federal and Secular Design'.
questions.a: Machinery mirrors values -- parliamentary accountability, federal balance, secular equal-respect, judicial guardianship.
